name: Oud and amber Middle Eastern fragrances
lead: Oud, or agarwood, is a resinous heartwood that forms in Aquilaria trees after infection by a mould; the tree produces resin as a defence and the wood darkens and becomes dense.[1] It is a popular perfume ingredient, usually used as a base note and traditionally paired with rose.[1] In the Arab world it is a long-standing aromatic burned as incense.[1]

"Amber" in perfumery refers both to a fragrance family and to ambergris, a waxy substance from sperm whales, now largely replaced by the synthetic ambroxide.[2][3] Alcohol-free attar perfumes are another traditional category associated with the Middle East and South Asia.[4]
infobox: Aquilaria listed in CITES Appendix II
Top-grade agarwood among the costliest natural materials

paras: More than 150 compounds have been identified in agarwood oil, at least 70 of them terpenoids, with the profile varying by species, tree age and extraction.[1] Few houses use real oud because it is costly and potent, so many products use accords built from synthetic components, and oil is often diluted with cheaper materials such as patchouli.[1] The article cites first-grade agarwood as among the most expensive natural materials in the world.[1]

Use spans thousands of years, including ancient Egyptian funerary use and mention in India's Vedas, and it was valued in Chinese, Japanese and Vietnamese trade and medicine.[1] Aquilaria malaccensis has been in CITES Appendix II since 1995 and all Aquilaria species since 2004.[1]

Ambergris was prized as a fixative that makes scents last longer; ambrein oxidises into ambroxide and ambrinol, its main odour components, and ambroxide is now made synthetically.[2] Its legal status varies: possession and trade are prohibited in the US, Australia and India, but permitted in the UK, EU and Switzerland.[2]

Attar is an oil-based perfume traditionally distilled onto a wood base such as sandalwood and aged for one to ten years; it is classed as "warm" (musk, amber, saffron) or "cool" (rose, jasmine, khus).[4] Musk Tahara is a personal fragrance used in the Muslim world for grooming and ritual, now mostly made with synthetic musk.[4] Al-Kindi's 9th-century book described over a hundred perfume recipes, and Ibn Sina popularised flower distillation.[5]

Oud and amber-heavy Arabian-style fragrances are discussed in fragrance communities as strong, long-lasting and distinct from Western designer scents. Specific community sources were not available for citation.

card.summary: Rich resinous and ambery scents rooted in Middle Eastern perfumery; much "oud" in stores is synthetic.
card.note: Real oud and ambergris involve conservation and legal issues; no attractiveness studies.

quick.overview:
Oud is a fragrant resinous wood used in Arab perfumery for centuries, often alongside amber and rose. It has become a trend in fragrance communities.

Many commercial oud scents use synthetic accords because real oud is rare and costly.
quick.mechanism: Fragrances use oud, amber-type notes and attars as long-lasting base notes.
quick.risks: Wild agarwood is protected under CITES and ambergris trade is restricted in some countries. Fragrance ingredients can cause allergies in some people.
